articles.title: Recovery in Ukraine, one life at a time
articles.summary: In classrooms, maternity wards, hospital corridors and local communities across Ukraine, people are rebuilding their lives despite the ongoing war.
articles.content:
In the frontline village of Bezruky which sits in the Kharkiv region – just half an hour’s drive from the Russian border – the local school took a direct hit early in the war and shut its doors. Tanks rolled past close enough to hear.

Rebuilt windows and a reinforced structure brought it back. The basement became something else entirely; a shelter, then a gallery.

© UNOPS/Veronika Yaresko

More than 15,000 children in the region are back in classrooms because of the project, run by the UN’s field agency for infrastructure and building projects (UNOPS) with European Union funding.

A curriculum built around the child

Teacher Yurii Tkalenko has spent 20 years in Cherkasy region classrooms. In 2025 he joined a training programme built around the New Ukrainian School reform.

“Learning never stops,” he says. “The new curriculum focuses on the child, adapting education to their needs.”

The programme is run by education and culture agency UNESCO, funded by the Global Partnership for Education, with Ukraine’s education ministry.

Mothers bring new hope

For Anastasiia, from the Donetsk region, having a baby meant leaving home for a protected maternity ward in Kharkiv, where she gave birth to twin boys.

“I was afraid to give birth. But life goes on,” she says. “The doctors truly brought us through.”

© UNFPA

The UN’s sexual and reproductive health agency UNFPA, working with the EU, backs maternity units like hers across the frontline.

Nannies, and a way back to work

Childcare is often what decides whether a mother can work at all. The ILO’s Nanny School has trained 80 women to care for children aged nought to three; nearly half found jobs soon after certifying.

It is a small programme, but one built to expand, moving women out of informal work and into something steadier.

In Kryvyi Rih, Oksana now drives one of the city’s longest bus routes, after training through UN Women’s She Drives project. She had worked as a cargo clerk and doubted she would even pass selection.

© UN Women

‘For many passengers, it’s still unusual to see a woman driving a bus, but their gratitude motivates me,’ she says. ‘If you want to do something, don’t be afraid to try. I wanted to change my life, and I did.’

‘We’re not alone’

In Zaporizhzhia, hospital director Hanna Makarenkova has spent the war treating blast injuries and receiving evacuees from Mariupol – more than 25,000 patients since the full-scale invasion began, often through bombardment and blackout.

‘My colleagues give me the strength to keep working,’ she says. ‘Their tireless work, their dedication to the cause, is what motivates me.’

New independent power units, funded by the EU and installed by UNDP, now keep her equipment running when the grid fails.

Restoring strength and hope

In Kostiantynivka, Oleksandr lost both legs and an eye in a drone strike. His wife, Nataliia, has spent three months at his side through surgery and relearning – how to balance, how to move into a wheelchair, with a physical therapist named Illia.

‘Movement is life,’ she says. Then, of the road ahead: ‘I think everything will be alright for us. We’ll live and enjoy life. Because life goes on.’

© WHO

The UN’s World health Organization (WHO), funded by the EU, has now trained more than 300 rehabilitation specialists across Ukraine to fit and adjust wheelchairs, nine of them now training others in turn.

None of this undoes what the war has taken. But it is what rebuilding looks like up close.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories

articles.personality_title: Communities in Ukraine rebuild lives amid war, step by step
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Ukraine has been facing a difficult war, especially near the Russian border. Many places, including schools and hospitals, were damaged or closed. Despite this, people are working hard to rebuild their daily lives.

**What happened** – In the village of Bezruky, near Kharkiv, a local school was hit early in the war but has since been repaired and reopened. More than 15,000 children returned to class thanks to help from the United Nations and European Union. Teachers are using new ways to teach that focus on each child’s needs. Mothers from war zones are giving birth in safe maternity wards supported by UN programs. Women are finding new jobs, like driving buses or caring for young children, through special training projects. Hospitals are treating thousands of patients and now have backup power systems to keep working during blackouts. People injured in the war are receiving rehabilitation to regain movement and independence.

**Impact** – These efforts show how communities are healing by focusing on education, healthcare, jobs, and recovery. For example, children returning to school help bring normal life back. Mothers getting safe care allow families to grow even during hard times. Training women for steady work helps families earn income. Rehabilitation for injured people gives them a chance to live more fully again. Each step helps build a stronger, more hopeful future.

**What’s next step** – These programs plan to keep growing and reaching more people. Teachers will continue to learn new methods. More women will be trained for jobs. Hospitals will maintain and improve services. Rehabilitation specialists will train others, spreading skills across the country. This ongoing work will help Ukraine recover, one person and one community at a time.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Despite war, Ukrainians are rebuilding their lives through education, healthcare, jobs, and rehabilitation, supported by UN and EU programs.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les communautés en Ukraine reconstruisent leur vie pas à pas malgré la guerre
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – L’Ukraine traverse une guerre difficile, notamment près de la frontière russe. De nombreux lieux, comme les écoles et les hôpitaux, ont été endommagés ou fermés. Malgré cela, les habitants travaillent dur pour reconstruire leur quotidien.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Dans le village de Bezruky, près de Kharkiv, une école locale a été touchée au début de la guerre mais a depuis été réparée et rouverte. Des mères venant des zones de guerre accouchent dans des maternités protégées soutenues par des programmes de l’ONU. Des femmes trouvent de nouveaux emplois, comme conduire des bus ou garder de jeunes enfants, grâce à des formations spécifiques. Les hôpitaux soignent des milliers de patients et disposent désormais de systèmes d’alimentation de secours pour fonctionner lors des coupures. Les personnes blessées reçoivent une rééducation pour retrouver mobilité et autonomie.

**Impact** – Ces actions montrent comment les communautés se reconstruisent en se concentrant sur l’éducation, la santé, l’emploi et la réadaptation. Par exemple, le retour des enfants à l’école aide à retrouver une vie normale. Les mères qui bénéficient de soins sûrs permettent aux familles de grandir malgré les difficultés. Former les femmes à des emplois stables aide les familles à gagner un revenu. La rééducation donne aux blessés une chance de mieux vivre. Chaque pas contribue à un avenir plus fort et plus optimiste.

**Prochaine étape** – Ces programmes continueront de se développer pour toucher plus de personnes. Les enseignants poursuivront leur formation. Plus de femmes seront formées pour travailler. Les hôpitaux maintiendront et amélioreront leurs services. Les spécialistes de la rééducation formeront d’autres personnes, diffusant leurs compétences dans tout le pays. Ce travail continu aidera l’Ukraine à se relever, une personne et une communauté à la fois.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Malgré la guerre, les Ukrainiens reconstruisent leur vie grâce à l’éducation, la santé, l’emploi et la rééducation, avec le soutien des programmes de l’ONU et de l’UE.
articles.personality_title_es: Comunidades en Ucrania reconstruyen sus vidas paso a paso a pesar de la guerra
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Ucrania enfrenta una guerra difícil, especialmente cerca de la frontera con Rusia. Muchos lugares, como escuelas y hospitales, fueron dañados o cerrados. A pesar de esto, la gente trabaja duro para reconstruir su vida diaria.

**Qué pasó** – En el pueblo de Bezruky, cerca de Járkov, una escuela local fue dañada al inicio de la guerra pero ya fue reparada y reabierta. Más de 15,000 niños regresaron a clases gracias a la ayuda de las Naciones Unidas y la Unión Europea. Los maestros usan nuevas formas de enseñar, enfocadas en las necesidades de cada niño. Madres de zonas de guerra dan a luz en maternidades seguras apoyadas por programas de la ONU. Mujeres encuentran nuevos trabajos, como conducir autobuses o cuidar niños pequeños, mediante programas de capacitación. Los hospitales atienden a miles de pacientes y ahora cuentan con sistemas de energía de respaldo para seguir funcionando durante cortes. Las personas heridas reciben rehabilitación para recuperar movimiento e independencia.

**Impacto** – Estos esfuerzos muestran cómo las comunidades se están recuperando al enfocarse en educación, salud, empleo y recuperación. Por ejemplo, el regreso de los niños a la escuela ayuda a traer de vuelta la vida normal. Las madres que reciben atención segura permiten que las familias crezcan aún en tiempos difíciles. Capacitar a mujeres para trabajos estables ayuda a las familias a obtener ingresos. La rehabilitación da a los heridos una oportunidad para vivir mejor. Cada paso ayuda a construir un futuro más fuerte y esperanzador.

**Próximo paso** – Estos programas planean seguir creciendo y llegar a más personas. Los profesores seguirán aprendiendo nuevos métodos. Más mujeres serán capacitadas para trabajar. Los hospitales mantendrán y mejorarán sus servicios. Los especialistas en rehabilitación entrenarán a otros, difundiendo habilidades en todo el país. Este trabajo continuo ayudará a Ucrania a recuperarse, una persona y una comunidad a la vez.

**Conclusión en una frase** – A pesar de la guerra, los ucranianos están reconstruyendo sus vidas mediante la educación, la salud, el empleo y la rehabilitación, con apoyo de programas de la ONU y la UE.

articles.title: ‘Mightily like insurrection’: Revisiting Trinidad’s first Emancipation Day
articles.summary: On Trinidad's first Emancipation Day in 1834, Africans were no longer slaves, but they were not yet free. Their quiet self-restraint may have thwarted a plot to postpone their liberation.
articles.content:
This article by Judy Raymond, produced after reading through contemporary records, first appeared in the Trinidad and Tobago Guardian on July 31, 2014. An edited version is being republished on Global Voices with permission.

The petit careme hadn’t come yet, and August 1, 1834, was real rainy-season weather. An all-day rain fell and flooded the streets of Port of Spain, but still a bewildered, bedraggled crowd stood for hours outside Government House.

There was an equal number of men and women, about 300 in all, some holding their children in their arms. They were field labourers, dressed in the ragged clothes they wore for work, but they had not brought their cutlasses to town, nor even sticks to help them along the muddy, cartwheel-rutted tracks that served as country roads.

Although the crowd outside was quiet, inside the government buildings there was turmoil, as colonial officials and planters fretted about how to react to the gathering outside, some arguing that its very quietness was a threat. In the course of the morning, the police and the militia cavalry charged at the crowd, who scattered, but reformed and would not disperse.

What they wanted was their free papers, that the king had sent for them.

It was Emancipation Day, now marked with a public holiday and commemorated as a glorious occasion. But on that day in 1834, the former slaves were left unsure what they had to celebrate. By the time the sun fizzled out behind the watery clouds, some had been arrested and marched off to the gaol, where they were flogged.

But a much worse outcome was narrowly averted. The gutters of Port of Spain might have run with blood as well as rainwater that day, and for the following week, had it not been for the commander of the garrison at St. James, whose restraint matched that of the people waiting in the rain.

Lieutenant Colonel Henry Hardy of His Majesty’s 19th Regiment of Foot died in Trinidad the following April, aged 50, and lies forgotten in an unmarked grave, but he is an unsung hero. The compassion, determination and good sense exercised by Hardy, as well as by the cheated former slaves, averted not only a possible massacre by the colonial authorities, but also what might have been a plot by the local planters to postpone the proclamation of emancipation.

EL Joseph, the British-born editor of the Port of Spain Gazette, wrote a planter’s-eye view account of Emancipation Day in his history of Trinidad — the first — published in 1838. “The negroes of Trinidad,” wrote Joseph, “behaved less riotously than those of some of the neighbouring colonies […] they shewed much resistance, but this, in most cases, was of a passive nature. The use of the cat-o-nine-tails convinced some of the most refractory that they were in the wrong […] Contrary to the desire of many, martial law was not proclaimed.”

Even in her much later History of the West Indian Islands of Trinidad and Tobago 1498-1900 (published in 1961), Gertrude Carmichael also writes disparagingly of what she describes as a rowdy, abusive mob. This is the version that is generally reported in modern histories and has become accepted as fact.

But according to two eyewitness accounts by English soldiers, the “negroes of Trinidad” showed no resistance at all. In fact, they were astonishingly restrained, despite what seemed to have been concerted attempts by the civilian authorities to provoke them into violent protest. It was because of this self-discipline on the part of the only semi-liberated former slaves that the declaration of martial law was patently unnecessary and was in the end narrowly avoided.

The former slaves — now termed apprentices — had gathered on what should have been their first day of freedom, when the Abolition of Colonial Slavery Act had come into force. But now, it seemed to them, the planters and the colonial government were trying to cheat them of their liberty.

When the ex-slaves gathered outside the government offices, they got a six for a nine. There was no grand proclamation, no celebration, official or otherwise, and little to celebrate.

Eventually, Governor Sir George Hill, followed by members of the council, came out onto the balcony to answer the questions of the disappointed people waiting patiently below.

“These people appeared to be a deputation from a few French Estates; and were for the most part very old men, old women, and children,” wrote Major Henry Capadose of the First West India Regiment, who was part of the British garrison stationed in Trinidad and was at Government House that day. He later wrote a book, Sixteen Years in the West Indies, about his tropical service.

It’s generally thought that Emancipation was proclaimed at the government buildings and rum bond on the wharf (the site of the Treasury Building today). But pictures of those offices (which burned down in 1932) show a long one-storey building.

Moreover, Capadose says: “HE, the Governor, Sir George Hill, followed by the members of council, the Judges and other official Gentlemen, had repaired to the balcony of the Council chamber to enquire into the cause of such an assemblage as then filled the Court Yard, below the building.” He makes repeated references to the balcony and the crowd below.

So the governor’s equivocal address — a far cry from a proclamation — must have been made at the old government buildings in Brunswick (now Woodford) Square, torn down a few years later to make way for the new one, designed by Richard Bridgens, that later became the Red House.

On that rainy Emancipation Day, one of the crowd, a young man, asked the governor, in French, what was going on, and why the managers and overseers on the estates — some of whom had come with them to Port of Spain — insisted the former slaves had to continue working.

Governor Hill told them, also in French, that while it was true they were no longer slaves, neither were they entirely free. They were “apprentices” — as if they now needed to learn the same skills they had been practising since they were old enough to walk (the tiniest members of the field gangs, who pulled up weeds and gathered grass for the livestock, started work at four years old). And for the next six years they would still be obliged to work for the same masters, unpaid, for 45 hours a week — and longer in crop season.

The Abolition of Colonial Slavery Act abolished slavery “throughout the British colonies on, from and after the First of August, 1834.” But — a huge but — it stipulated that only children under six were actually free from that date; older children and adult field workers were to serve as “apprentices” for another six years, and house slaves for four years more.

The people gathered in the rain took the bad news calmly, but would not obey the governor’s urging that they should “return quietly home, like good folks, and resume their avocations under employers who, doubtless would treat them kindly, and indeed the new laws ensured them good treatment.”

Other colonial officials repeated what Governor Hill had said, but the rain-sodden crowd remained.

“Pas de six ans, nous ne voulons pas de six ans, nous sommes libres, le Roi nous a donné la liberté!” they said. “No six years, we do not want six years, we are free, the King has given us our freedom!”

The crowd may have been sullen, but they were peaceable. They stood there in the rain and would not leave.

Some hot-headed members of the council wanted the governor to declare martial law and have the crowd dispersed by force. The militia had already been called out and were stationed at street corners, in case of insurrection.

In reality, points out Capadose, “No symptom of it appeared, beyond the obstinacy of foolish old people in the government courtyard, headed by a single young man, and none of them had even a stick in their hands.”

The governor consulted Colonel Hardy.

“Martial law!” exclaimed he, “Against whom? I see only old men, women, and children, poor ignorant people, who come to ask a question, and know no better.”

Given this answer, Governor Hill could not very well read the Riot Act. In the end, around sunset, the police persuaded the doleful apprentices to go home.

Capadose rode back to the St. James Barracks in Hardy’s carriage. They did see some celebrations on the way: “A number of girls danced about in the streets, singing French ariettes of, probably, their own composition on the goodness of King William in granting them freedom.”

Colonel Hardy observed drily that it “looked mightily like insurrection.”
articles.reasoning: The article recounts a historically significant moment marking the beginning of emancipation in Trinidad, highlighting the peaceful yet determined resistance of former slaves against continued oppression. It emphasizes the restraint and courage of the emancipated people and the crucial role of a military commander in averting violence, illustrating an important milestone in the struggle for freedom and human rights with broad social and historical significance.
articles.personality_title: Trinidad’s first Emancipation Day: peaceful courage amid uncertainty
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – On August 1, 1834, Trinidad marked its first Emancipation Day, the day when slavery officially ended in British colonies. However, former slaves were not fully free yet. They became “apprentices,” required to work without pay for several more years under their former masters.

**What happened** – Despite heavy rain, about 300 former slaves gathered quietly outside Government House in Port of Spain, seeking proof of their freedom. They were patient but firm, refusing to leave when officials delayed giving clear answers. Some colonial leaders wanted to use force, but the crowd stayed peaceful. Lieutenant Colonel Henry Hardy, a British army officer, advised against violence, helping to avoid a possible massacre.

**Impact** – This event showed the strength and self-control of the newly freed people, who faced unfair treatment but chose peaceful protest over violence. It also revealed how close the situation came to becoming violent, and how one person’s calm leadership helped prevent bloodshed. The day was not the joyful celebration it is now, but it marked the start of a long journey toward true freedom.

**What’s next step** – The former slaves entered a difficult apprenticeship period lasting up to six years, still working without pay but slowly gaining rights. Over time, this system was abolished, leading to full freedom. Today, Emancipation Day is a public holiday in Trinidad, remembering both the struggles and the peaceful courage shown that day.

**One-sentence takeaway** – On Trinidad’s first Emancipation Day, peaceful resistance and wise leadership prevented violence and began the path from slavery to freedom.
articles.personality_title_fr: Première Journée de l’Émancipation à Trinidad : courage pacifique dans l’incertitude
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le 1er août 1834, Trinidad célébrait sa première Journée de l’Émancipation, marquant officiellement la fin de l’esclavage dans les colonies britanniques. Cependant, les anciens esclaves n’étaient pas encore complètement libres. Ils devenaient des « apprentis », contraints de travailler gratuitement pendant plusieurs années pour leurs anciens maîtres.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Malgré une forte pluie, environ 300 anciens esclaves se sont rassemblés calmement devant la Government House à Port of Spain, demandant une preuve de leur liberté. Ils étaient patients mais déterminés, refusant de partir lorsque les autorités retardaient les réponses. Certains dirigeants coloniaux voulaient utiliser la force, mais la foule est restée pacifique. Le lieutenant-colonel Henry Hardy, officier de l’armée britannique, a conseillé d’éviter la violence, aidant à prévenir un massacre.

**Impact** – Cet événement a montré la force et la maîtrise de soi des nouveaux libres, qui ont fait face à une injustice mais ont choisi la protestation pacifique. Il a aussi révélé combien la situation a failli devenir violente, et comment le calme d’une personne a évité le sang versé. Ce jour n’était pas une fête joyeuse comme aujourd’hui, mais il marquait le début d’un long chemin vers la vraie liberté.

**Étape suivante** – Les anciens esclaves ont entamé une période difficile d’apprentissage pouvant durer jusqu’à six ans, toujours sans salaire mais avec des droits progressifs. Ce système a ensuite été aboli, menant à la liberté complète. Aujourd’hui, la Journée de l’Émancipation est un jour férié à Trinidad, en mémoire des luttes et du courage pacifique de ce jour.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Le premier jour de l’émancipation à Trinidad a vu une résistance pacifique et un leadership sage éviter la violence et ouvrir la voie de l’esclavage à la liberté.
articles.personality_title_es: Primer Día de la Emancipación en Trinidad: coraje pacífico en medio de la incertidumbre
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El 1 de agosto de 1834, Trinidad celebró su primer Día de la Emancipación, cuando la esclavitud terminó oficialmente en las colonias británicas. Sin embargo, los antiguos esclavos no eran aún completamente libres. Se convirtieron en “aprendices”, obligados a trabajar sin pago durante varios años para sus antiguos amos.

**Qué pasó** – A pesar de la lluvia intensa, unas 300 personas se reunieron en silencio frente a la Casa de Gobierno en Puerto España, buscando pruebas de su libertad. Fueron pacientes pero firmes, negándose a irse cuando las autoridades retrasaban respuestas claras. Algunos líderes coloniales querían usar la fuerza, pero la multitud permaneció pacífica. El teniente coronel Henry Hardy, oficial del ejército británico, aconsejó evitar la violencia y ayudó a prevenir una masacre.

**Impacto** – Este evento mostró la fuerza y el autocontrol de las personas recién liberadas, que enfrentaron un trato injusto pero eligieron la protesta pacífica. También reveló cuán cerca estuvo la situación de volverse violenta y cómo un liderazgo tranquilo evitó derramamiento de sangre. Ese día no fue una celebración alegre como hoy, pero marcó el inicio de un largo camino hacia la verdadera libertad.

**Próximo paso** – Los antiguos esclavos entraron en un período difícil de aprendizaje que duró hasta seis años, trabajando sin paga pero ganando derechos poco a poco. Con el tiempo, este sistema fue abolido y llegó la libertad completa. Hoy, el Día de la Emancipación es un día festivo en Trinidad, recordando las luchas y el coraje pacífico de aquel día.

**Frase clave** – En el primer Día de la Emancipación en Trinidad, la resistencia pacífica y el liderazgo sabio evitaron la violencia y comenzaron el camino de la esclavitud a la libertad.
